track.name: operations
track.label: Operations & Process
track.summary: Go from process mapping and Lean fundamentals to running projects, supply chains, and dashboards that keep a growing organization from falling over — the operating discipline every business function eventually needs.

phases.title: Operations Fundamentals & Process Thinking
phases.description: What operations management actually covers, how to see a process clearly on paper, and the strategic tradeoffs that shape how it should run.

phases.title: Lean & Process Improvement
phases.description: The Lean and Six Sigma toolkit for finding waste, fixing root causes, and making improvement a habit instead of a one-off project.

phases.title: Project & Program Management
phases.description: Running a single project well, adapting Agile methods outside of software teams, and coordinating work across departments that don't report to each other.

phases.title: Supply Chain & Operations Planning
phases.description: How goods and information move from suppliers to customers, and the forecasting and vendor decisions that keep that flow reliable.

phases.title: Operational Metrics & Performance Management
phases.description: Turning operations into numbers worth looking at: dashboards, root-cause tools, and documentation that outlives any one person's memory.

phases.title: Scaling Operations & Change Management
phases.description: What breaks first as a company grows, how to get people to actually adopt a new process, and where automation earns its keep.

topics.title: Deciding What to Measure, and Getting the Data
topics.description: Where dashboard numbers come from: picking the measure, instrumenting the process, and checking the data is true.

steps.t: Pick one leading and one lagging measure
steps.d: For a single process, name one measure that predicts trouble and one that records the result. Two, not twelve.
Exactly what counts, from when to when, and what is excluded. Undefined metrics get argued about instead of acted on.

steps.t: Decide where the number comes from
steps.d: A system log, a form someone fills in, or a count at a station. Name the source and who is responsible for it.

steps.t: Measure it by hand for a week
steps.d: Before building anything. A week of manual counts tells you whether the definition survives contact with the process.

steps.t: Check the data against reality once
steps.d: Compare the recorded figure with a physical count or a second source. Most dashboards are wrong at this step, not the charting step.

topics.title: What operations management is
topics.description: The function that turns strategy into repeatable, efficient delivery of a product or service.

steps.d: Name the five main functions an operations team runs (production, distribution, service delivery, safety/quality, planning) and pick one that exists in your own organization.

steps.t: Map a strategy to an operation
steps.d: Take a business strategy (low-cost leader, premium quality, fast response) and write how operations would need to differ to support it.
Find one company's annual report and identify which operational priorities its strategy actually reveals (speed, cost, flexibility, quality).
In a process you know well (a job function, a customer service workflow, production), name the single biggest bottleneck that slows everything else down.
Take a real business failure (a recall, a service outage, a bankruptcy) and analyze whether it was an operational failure or a strategy failure.

topics.title: Process Mapping & Value Stream Analysis
topics.description: Drawing a process as it actually runs — not as people assume it does — to see where time and value get lost.

steps.d: For a process you do weekly, map the Suppliers, Inputs, Process steps, Outputs, and Customers on paper or in a simple spreadsheet.
Draw or photograph your process as it actually runs (not as the manual says), labeling each step, wait time, and decision point.
Track how long a single item (order, document, customer request) takes to move through the entire process and how far it physically travels.
Compare your current map to the ideal: highlight steps that add no value, inventory that waits, and handoffs that cause delays.
Redraw the process eliminating the three biggest waste points you found, and estimate how much time or cost that saves.

topics.title: Operations Strategy & the Efficiency-Flexibility Tradeoff
topics.description: Why an operation optimized for low cost and one optimized for adaptability tend to pull in different directions.

steps.d: For one product or service, list whether the company is optimized for low cost, high quality, speed, or flexibility.
Pick two competing priorities (cost vs. quality, or speed vs. flexibility) and write how investing in one makes the other harder.
Take a low-cost operation (a fast-food chain, a discount retailer) and name three operational choices that drive down cost.
Think of a business or project where pursuing one priority broke another (e.g., cutting staff broke quality; quality standards broke speed).
Take a company that chose wrong (too much cost-cutting, too much quality-chasing) and describe how you'd shift it back toward balance.

topics.title: Lean Principles & Waste Elimination
topics.description: Seeing a process through the lens of value versus the eight wastes of Lean.

steps.d: Using the DOWNTIME framework (Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilized talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Extra-processing), find one example of each in a process you know.
Watch or trace one cycle of a real process and mark every moment that doesn't add value to the customer.
Quantify one waste: calculate how many hours per week are spent waiting, reworking, or moving things that the customer doesn't care about.
If you eliminated the largest single waste, how much time, money, or capacity would you free up?
Pick the biggest waste and sketch one change (a process step, a tool, a rule) that would eliminate it without adding cost elsewhere.

topics.title: Six Sigma & DMAIC
topics.description: A structured, data-driven cycle — Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control — for fixing a process that isn't meeting expectations.

steps.d: Take a process that's not meeting a target (late delivery, high defect rate, cost overruns) and write a specific problem statement with numbers.
Collect 30-50 data points on the metric you care about to establish a baseline: time, defects, cost, or quality score.
Use a Fishbone diagram or Pareto analysis to find the 2-3 factors responsible for 80% of the problem.
Run a one-week trial of your proposed fix on a subset of the process and measure whether the metric actually improved.
Measure performance two weeks after rolling out the fix, document the new standard operating procedure, and train the team on it.

topics.title: Kaizen & Continuous Improvement
topics.description: Small, constant changes made by the people doing the work, instead of one big overhaul.

steps.d: Bring together 5-8 people who actually do the work and spend one day mapping, analyzing, and proposing small changes to a single process.
List 10 small changes (reorder a workstation, add a checklist, combine two approval steps) that each person can implement in under an hour.
For the next month, implement one small improvement per week, measure its impact, and keep the ones that work.
Record the time saved, defect reduction, or cost cut from each small change and add them up over 12 weeks.
Create a standing 30-minute meeting where the team reviews last week's changes, celebrates wins, and proposes next week's experiments.

topics.title: Project Management Fundamentals (scope/schedule/budget)
topics.description: The triple constraint every project manager balances, and why moving one side of it moves the other two.

steps.d: Write what the project will deliver, what it will not touch, and the acceptance criteria (specific enough that you'd know when it's done).
List every major phase from start to finish and estimate how long each one will take, including buffer time.
Estimate labor (by role and hours), materials, and overhead, then sum them to get a total budget with a contingency.
Assume the schedule gets cut by 25%: write which two of scope or budget would have to change, and why.
Present your scope, schedule, and budget to someone skeptical and explain why you can't shrink all three at once.

topics.title: Agile & Scrum for Operations
topics.description: Borrowing sprints, backlogs, and standups for operational work that isn't software development.

steps.d: Take operational work you know (onboarding, process audit, vendor review) and break it into stories and tasks small enough to finish in a sprint.
Run a 15-minute daily standup with three people discussing what they finished yesterday, what's next, and what's blocking them.
Set up a simple three-column board (To Do, In Progress, Done) and move sticky notes as tasks advance through your sprint.
At the end of a sprint, gather your team and list what went well, what didn't, and one thing to change next sprint.
Count the story points or hours you completed in your first sprint, then do it again for three more sprints and track the trend.

topics.title: Managing Cross-Functional Projects
topics.description: Getting people who don't share a manager, incentives, or vocabulary to ship something together.

steps.d: Invite one leader from each function (ops, finance, marketing, etc.) to own a cross-functional project, define success together, and unblock the work.
Write a single project objective that all functions agree on, even if they have different success measures underneath it.
List every handoff and dependency between functions: what Marketing needs from Ops before they can move forward, and vice versa.
Take a real decision where two functions want different things and use your steering committee to make an explicit choice and document the tradeoff.
Complete a cross-functional project (even a small pilot or 30-day sprint) and deliver it on time, with sign-off from all functions.

topics.title: Supply Chain Fundamentals
topics.description: The network of suppliers, manufacturers, and distributors that gets a product to a customer, and what managing it actually involves.

steps.d: Draw or list every step from your top three suppliers to delivery to a customer, including warehouses, manufacturing, and transport.
For each major input to your process, find the supplier with the longest lead time and list what could break if they fail.
Add up the time from raw material order through manufacturing to delivery to find your total supply-chain lead time.
Of all the steps in your chain, which one takes the longest, costs the most, or has the worst on-time rate?
For your biggest supply-chain risk (single supplier, long lead time, poor track record), propose a concrete change (redundancy, local sourcing, inventory).

topics.title: Inventory Management & Demand Forecasting
topics.description: Predicting what customers will want and deciding how much stock to hold without tying up cash unnecessarily.

steps.d: Use 12-24 months of past sales data to forecast next quarter's demand using a simple method (average, trend line, or seasonal adjustment).
For one product, find the Economic Order Quantity by balancing ordering costs against holding costs.
Calculate safety stock if you assume 95% service level vs. 99%, and compare the inventory and cost difference.
If demand suddenly doubled (or halved) tomorrow, how many weeks could you serve customers with your current inventory?
Identify one SKU or product family that's overstocked and describe how you'd cut inventory while protecting service level.

topics.title: Vendor & Procurement Management
topics.description: Choosing, contracting with, and managing the outside suppliers an operation depends on.

steps.d: For your top three vendors, create a simple scorecard (cost, quality, on-time delivery, responsiveness) and rate each 1-5.
Take one existing vendor relationship and propose one change (price, payment terms, quality SLA, minimum order, delivery frequency).
For one category of spend, invite at least two alternative suppliers to bid and compare their cost, terms, and capability.
Visit or request a tour of one of your critical vendors and document their capacity, processes, and risk (financial health, key person risk).
If one of your suppliers suddenly became unreliable, describe your contingency plan: alternatives, timeline, and cost to activate.

topics.title: Building an Operations Dashboard (KPIs/OKRs)
topics.description: Picking the handful of metrics that actually tell you whether an operation is healthy, and framing them as goals people can act on.

steps.d: For your operation, identify 6-8 metrics that matter (on-time delivery, defect rate, cost per unit, throughput, cycle time, utilization, customer satisfaction).
Of your list, choose the four that best signal whether the operation is healthy, measurable weekly, and actionable by the team.
For each KPI, write a quarterly target, a current value, and name one person accountable for moving it.
Create a simple dashboard (spreadsheet, one-page visual, or management tool) showing all four KPIs with trend lines and color coding.
Run a 30-minute weekly operations review, discuss each KPI, surface problems, and decide on actions or escalations.

topics.title: Root Cause Analysis (5 Whys, Fishbone)
topics.description: Simple tools for tracing a problem back to its actual cause instead of patching a symptom.

steps.d: Take a recurring issue (high defects, late delivery, customer complaints) and quantify it with a baseline number and a time period.
Start with your problem, ask why it happens, then why to that answer, repeating five times until you get past obvious symptoms.
Map possible causes of your problem across categories (People, Process, Materials, Environment, Methods) and pick the most likely three.
Design a small test to see if your suspected cause actually drives the problem: ask the team, run an experiment, or pull data.
If your root cause is correct, write one operational change that would eliminate it and estimate the impact on your problem metric.

topics.title: SOPs & Process Documentation
topics.description: Writing down how a process works so it survives someone leaving or a team growing.

steps.d: Pick a routine operational task (invoice a customer, onboard a vendor, handle a complaint) and write out every step in order.
For any step where someone has to decide, write the rule (if X, then Y; if not, then Z) so the next person knows what to do.
Walk through your SOP and list what could go wrong at each step (wrong person, wrong data, lost step, forgotten approval).
Name the person or role responsible for each step and for keeping this SOP current when the process changes.
Hand your documented process to someone who's never done it and watch them follow it; fix any steps that are unclear or wrong.

topics.title: Scaling Processes as a Company Grows
topics.description: Why what worked at 10 people breaks at 100, and how to rebuild a process before it breaks in production.

steps.d: Take a process that works at your current scale (10 people, $1M revenue) and list every assumption it makes about size and complexity.
Double your scale mentally: which one assumption would break first, and what would you have to change to fix it?
Rewrite one critical process to work at 10x your current size (tool changes, more oversight, specialization, automation).
List the top five things you'd rebuild before you hit the next major growth milestone (team size, revenue, customer count).
Try your redesigned process with a larger team or on a larger subset of work and measure whether it actually survives the scale.

topics.title: Change Management Fundamentals (ADKAR/Kotter)
topics.description: Two well-known models for getting people to actually adopt a new process instead of quietly reverting to the old one.

steps.d: For a process change you're planning, list why each group (frontline, supervisors, management, customers) might resist it.
For one change, write how you'll build Awareness (why we're changing), Desire (benefits), Knowledge (training), Ability (practice), Reinforcement (habit).
Start the new process with 20% of your people (the early adopters), document what works and what needs fixing, then expand.
Design and deliver training on the new process: show why it's better, demonstrate how it works, and practice it with feedback.
After two weeks, pull data on adoption rates and outcomes; if it's working, remove the old process, update documentation, and celebrate the win.

topics.title: Automation & Operational Tooling
topics.description: Deciding which repetitive operational work is worth automating, and with what kind of tool.

steps.d: For one week, list every task a team member spends more than 30 minutes on that's repetitive (same data entry, report, approval sequence).
Calculate how many labor hours per month are spent on the repetitive work, then multiply by hourly cost to get the annual burden.
For the costliest repetitive task, research three automation options (software, RPA, scripting, IFTTT) and their implementation cost and time.
Pick the quickest win (cheapest, least risk) and implement it for one process or one part of the workflow.
Track time saved and compare it to automation cost to calculate payback period; then decide whether to roll out or try a different task.
